source.title: On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures

accepted.question_text: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀ for some integer ν₀ ≥ 1. Define T on positive integers by T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 when n is odd. A cycle is a finite orbit Ω with T^k(x)=x for every x in Ω; C(a,b) is the set of all cycles. For a cycle Ω(ω) whose smallest element is ω, let G(ω) be the set of starting values that eventually reach ω, and let G(∞) be the set of starting values whose iterates diverge to infinity. Is C(a,b) always finite, with the positive integers decomposing as the union of the finitely many cycle basins G(ω₁*), …, G(ω_q*) and the possible divergent set G(∞)?
accepted.context_brief: Finiteness and basin decomposition for generalized Syracuse maps

evidence.quote: We consider the map T : N − → N given by T (n) = { n/ 2 if n is even , (an + b)/ 2 if n is odd , (2) where a and b are both odd integers such that a > − b.

A cycle of the graph associated to the map T having k vertices is a trajectory Ω for which T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω. The cardinal #Ω = Card (Ω) = k, also called the length, of Ω is in fact the smallest integer such that T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω.
G(ω ) = { n ∈ N : ∃ k ∈ N, T (k)(n) = ω } , and G(∞ ) = { n ∈ N : lim k→∞ T (k)(n) = ∞} .

Conjecture 2.1. For any parameters a and b such that a + b = 2 ν 0, where ν 0 ≥ 1, the set C(a, b ) has ﬁnite cardinality: 1 ≤ q∗ = # C(a, b ) < ∞ . Then, it follows that there is q∗ distinct integers ω ∗ 1, . . . , ω ∗ q∗ such that: C(a, b ) = { Ω(ω ∗ 1), . . . , Ω(ω ∗ q∗) } , and N = G(ω ∗ 1) ∪ · · · ∪ G(ω ∗ q∗ ) ∪ G(∞ ). The set G(∞ ) may be empty or not empty.

accepted.question_text: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. Let G(∞) be the set of positive starting values n for which T^k(n) tends to infinity. Which conditions on a and b make G(∞) empty, and which conditions make G(∞) nonempty? Equivalently, for which such maps does every trajectory eventually enter a finite cycle rather than diverge?
accepted.context_brief: Divergent trajectories in generalized Syracuse maps

evidence.quote: We consider the map T : N − → N given by T (n) = { n/ 2 if n is even , (an + b)/ 2 if n is odd , (2) where a and b are both odd integers such that a > − b.
G(ω ) = { n ∈ N : ∃ k ∈ N, T (k)(n) = ω } , and G(∞ ) = { n ∈ N : lim k→∞ T (k)(n) = ∞} .

Questions: Suppose that the condition a + b = 2 ν 0 holds, then one can ask the following questions: 1. Under which conditions on the parameters a and b the set G(∞ ) is empty or not empty? In this case where the set G(∞ ) is empty, there is no divergent trajectory.

accepted.question_text: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. If C(a,b) denotes the set of cycles of T on the positive integers, can one find effective estimates or bounds for the cardinality #C(a,b) that are strong enough to determine, or at least confirm, whether C(a,b) is finite?

evidence.quote: We consider the map T : N − → N given by T (n) = { n/ 2 if n is even , (an + b)/ 2 if n is odd , (2) where a and b are both odd integers such that a > − b.

A cycle of the graph associated to the map T having k vertices is a trajectory Ω for which T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω. The cardinal #Ω = Card (Ω) = k, also called the length, of Ω is in fact the smallest integer such that T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω.
2. Is it possible to ﬁnd an estimate for the cardinality # C(a, b )? Then, it will be possible to conﬁrm that the set C(a, b ) is ﬁnite.

accepted.question_text: Let a and b be odd integers with a > −b and a + b = 2^ν₀, and let T(n)=n/2 for even n and T(n)=(a n+b)/2 for odd n. Under which conditions on a and b does T have exactly one cycle, #C(a,b)=1? In that case, is the unique cycle necessarily the trivial cycle Ω(1), and, if G(∞)=∅ as well, does every positive integer n satisfy T^k(n)=1 for some k, so that all positive integers lie in G(1)?

evidence.quote: We consider the map T : N − → N given by T (n) = { n/ 2 if n is even , (an + b)/ 2 if n is odd , (2) where a and b are both odd integers such that a > − b.

A cycle of the graph associated to the map T having k vertices is a trajectory Ω for which T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω. The cardinal #Ω = Card (Ω) = k, also called the length, of Ω is in fact the smallest integer such that T (k)(x) = x for all x ∈ Ω.
G(ω ) = { n ∈ N : ∃ k ∈ N, T (k)(n) = ω } , and G(∞ ) = { n ∈ N : lim k→∞ T (k)(n) = ∞} .

3. Under which conditions on the parameters a and b, the set C(a, b ) is of cardinality #C(a, b ) = 1 ? In this case, we will see that the unique cycle in C(a, b ) is the trivial one Ω(1). If in addition G(∞ ) = ∅ , then for any integer n there exists an integer k such that T (k)(n) = 1 and we will have N = G(1).

accepted.question_text: For the classical Collatz/Syracuse map T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=(3n+1)/2 when n is odd, is Ω(1)=(1→2→1) the only cycle, and does every positive integer eventually reach 1, so that N=G(1) and there are no divergent trajectories G(∞)=∅?
accepted.context_brief: Classical Collatz conjecture in Syracuse-map notation

evidence.quote: The well-known conjecture of the 3 x+1 problem (or Collatz’s conjecture ) states that, for any initial value n ∈ N, there is a positive integer k ∈ N0 such that S(k)(n) = 1. A second conjecture in the Syracuse problem states that the trivial c ycle (1 → 2 → 1) is the unique cycle in the graph associated to the map S.

Conjecture 2.2. (Collatz conjecture) For the parameters a = 3 and b = 1 the set C(3, 1) contains only one cycle (the trivial one): C(3, 1) = { Ω(1)} , with Ω(1) = (1 → 2 → 1) and we have: N = G(1) and G(∞ ) = ∅ .

accepted.question_text: For every integer ν≥1 with ν≠2, define T(n)=n/2 when n is even and T(n)=((2^ν−1)n+(2^ν+1))/2 when n is odd, and set b=2^ν+1. Is C(2^ν−1,2^ν+1) exactly the two cycles Ω(1)=(1→2^ν→2^{ν−1}→…→2→1) and Ω(b)=(b→2^{ν−1}b→2^{ν−2}b→…→2b→b)? Is N=G(1)∪G(b)∪G(∞), with G(∞)=∅ for ν=1 and G(∞)≠∅ for ν≥3?

We have C(a, b ) = { Ω(1), Ω(b)} , and N = G(1) ∪ G(b) ∪ G(∞ ), with G(∞ ) = ∅ for ν = 1 and G(∞ ) ̸= ∅ for ν ≥ 3. The trivial cycle of length ν + 1 is Ω(1) = (1 → 2ν → 2ν − 1 → 2ν − 2 → . . . 2 → 1), and the second cycle of length ν is Ω(b) = ( b → 2ν − 1b → 2ν − 2b → . . . → 2b → b).

needs_review.question_text_raw: If a nontrivial cycle Ω with m oscillations exists in the generalized Syracuse map with b≥1, what lower bounds must m satisfy?

evidence.quote: In [11], Simons and Weger derived lower and upper bounds for hypothetical cycle with m oscillations. A cycle with m oscillations contains m local minimum odd integers x0, x1, . . . , x m− 1 and m local maximum even integers y0, y1, . . . , y m− 1
Theorem 4.1. Let us set c1 = (a − 2) log(2) b with b ≥ 1. If a nontrivial cycle Ω with m oscillations exists, then for all n ≥ 1, m ≥ min ( qn, c1 min(Ω) qn + qn+1 ).

Theorem 4.2. Let us set c1 = a log(2) b with b ≥ 1. If a nontrivial cycle Ω with m oscillations exists, then for all n ≥ 1, there exists an integer n0 > 0 such that for all n ≥ n0, we have m ≥ min ( qn, c1 min(Ω) qµ n ), where µ is a measure of irrationality of log(a) log(2) .

needs_review.question_text_raw: For the family T(n)=n/2 if n is even and T(n)=((2^ν+1)n+(2^ν−1))/2 if n is odd, can a nontrivial one-oscillation cycle exist?

evidence.quote: Theorem 5.2. Let ν ≥ 1 and let the parameters a = 2ν + 1 and b = 2ν − 1, a necessary condition that a nontrivial cycle Ω for T having one oscillation exists is that there exists an integer n0 > 0 such that for K > n 0, we have 2K − 1 ≤ K µ log(2) , L = 1 − K + ⌊ log(a) log(2) K ⌋ and aK − 2K 2K+L − aK ∈ N, where µ is a measure of irrationality of log(a) log(2) , K and L are the number of odd and even integers in the cycle Ω, respectively.

Corollary 5.1. For ν = 1, we get the classical case of the Syracuse problem correspon ding to a = 3 and b = 1. In this case, it follows that there is no cycle with only one o scillation other than the trivial cycle.

Mapped an 18-page PDF titled 'On a general Syracuse problem with conjectures'; explicit open-problem regions are Conjectures 2.1, 2.2, 5.1-5.7 and the Questions block on page 3; implicit conditional regions occur in Sections 4 and 5.1.
Introduction states the classical Collatz convergence and uniqueness conjectures; merged these into q_005 because Conjecture 2.2 restates them in the paper's notation.
Section 2 defines T, cycles, C(a,b), G(ω), and G(∞), then yields Conjecture 2.1 plus three explicit questions and the Collatz conjecture.
Section 3 gives lower bounds for hypothetical cycle lengths but does not formulate a standalone open question beyond already extracted cycle-existence conjectures.

Section 4 contains conditional results about hypothetical m-oscillation cycles; retained one implicit candidate in needs_review because the source states conditions rather than a complete open question.

Section 5 supplies seven explicit family-specific conjectures and one implicit one-oscillation candidate; extracted Conjectures 5.1-5.7 as q_006-q_012 and retained the implicit one-oscillation item for review.
